claims.text: Cold spray additive repair will restore the damaged component's performance under aggressive operating conditions.
Avoiding the high temperatures of traditional fusion welding will prevent hot cracking during repair.
The component material has a microstructure susceptible to hot cracking during high-temperature processing.
The localized damage compromises component performance.
Cold spray accelerates metal powder to high velocities and deposits it on the damaged region.
Cold spray can deposit the repair material without melting the substrate.
Controlled low-temperature deposition will avoid alteration of the base-material microstructure.
The repaired component is intended to operate under aggressive mechanical loading and elevated temperatures within the material's operational limits.
Cold spray will produce a dense, well-bonded repair layer with an effective substrate interface.
The repair layer will maintain structural integrity and mitigate crack propagation.
High-velocity particle impacts cause plastic deformation and adhesion to the substrate.
Cold spray avoids formation of a fusion zone.
Avoiding a fusion zone reduces thermal stresses associated with hot cracking.
The cold-sprayed repair will have strength and fatigue resistance at least equal to those of a traditional fusion-welded repair.
The cold-sprayed repair will eliminate hot-cracking risk relative to fusion-welded repair.
Cold-spray repair will extend the component's service life.
Traditional fusion-welding repair is ineffective for this material because of hot-cracking risk and possible microstructural degradation.
Applicability of the repair depends on component geometry, material compatibility with controlled cold-spray deposition, and optimization of repair-layer thickness.
Performance under extreme cyclic or impact loading and long-term environmental exposure remains unverified.
